notes: West leads the ♥Q against 3NT. West's opening heart lead is won in dummy with the ♥A. There are 8 top tricks (the ♠A, 2 hearts, only 3 diamond due to the blockage, and 2 clubs). Both spades and clubs offer prospects for a ninth trick.

South can only afford to give up the lead once as the defense will be able to establish and run the hearts. South might think about ducking a club to the defense at trick 2. This line of play will succeed whenever clubs are 3-3. A 3-3 break occurs about 36% of the time. South can do better by playing a spade to the ♠J at trick 2.

The contract will immediately succeed when East began with both the ♠K and ♠Q (24%). South will also succeed on several other distributions of the defensive spades. If, for example, East holds a doubleton spade honour, West will win the first spade trick, but South's ♠A will later drop East's doubleton honour. The odds of East holding a doubleton honour in spades are about 13%.
When you factor in the other spade holdings (the above holding for example) that allow the contract to make, the spade play becomes better than playing on clubs by about 6%.

There is a third line of play that combines the chances in both spades and clubs. South can achieve almost the same odds of success as playing a spade to the ♠J by playing the ♠A at trick 2. If an honour drops, South can develop his ninth trick by continuing spades.

If both defenders follow small, South switches his attack to clubs, making the contract when clubs are 3-3. This line of play is only inferior to playing a spade to the ♠J by about one quarter of 1%. As these lines of play are so close, you will be rewarded by taking either line.

On the second last diamond, West can painlessly let go of a club and dummy is squeezed. Whatever is discarded from dummy, the defense will be able to come to another trick. It would have made no difference if the ♣A had been cashed earlier.

If South wins the heart shift with the ♥K in dummy, the squeeze will function. After finessing in spades, South runs his winners to reach the above position. On the last diamond, West must discard a heart in order to guard clubs. A club now can be thrown from dummy while East discards a spade. On the play of a club to the ♣A, East is squeezed. A spade discard will set up dummy's spade. As East now has the sole defensive heart guard, a heart discard is also fatal.

In every double squeeze, declarer must have a winner in the suit that both defenders are to be squeezed in. The entry requirements when there is only 1 such winner are very delicate. West's trick 2 heart shift was an attempt to disrupt this mechanism.

There must be at least 1 winner in the shared suit at the time of the squeeze. Double squeezes mature with 1 loser. Several forms of double squeeze exist. South will continue by unblocking in spades and running the clubs (it does not matter if the ♦A is cashed first). Discarding the ♥Q or ♥J allows East to build a heart trick by covering with the ♥K when the ♥10 is led.

South's duck "on general principles" at trick 1 was wrong. The contract depends strictly on the heart finesse. By ducking at trick 1, South is rectifying the count for a one-suit squeeze against himself. The hand plays very simply if the ♦A is won at trick 1.

South unblocks the spades as before and runs the clubs. On the play of the ♠Q, South can painlessly discard the ♦J. The ♥10 is played next. Whether or not East plays the ♥K, South will lose only 1 trick at the end.

notes: West leads the ♦J against 6NT. West's opening lead is won by South. South should play to take 5 spades tricks by finessing twice, 2 heart tricks once the ♥A is knocked out, 3 diamond tricks, and 2 club tricks.

A heart should be played at once. When the defender with the ♥A ducks, South should take advantage of this dummy entry and finesse in spades. When the finesse wins, South will succeed easily unless East started with 5 spades. In this case, if East has length in clubs, South may be able to squeeze East for his twelfth trick.

Another heart is played. If West wins the ♥A, a simple squeeze will operate. Assume West returns a club. South wins in dummy, cashes dummy's heart winner for a club discard, and cashes the remaining diamonds.
East is squeezed on the third round of diamonds. A spade discard will allow South to run the suit after taking a second finesse. A club discard will establish dummy's club suit.

Therefore, West will duck the second heart trick, refusing to rectify the count. South then can succeed with a strip squeeze. A second spade finesse is taken. When West discards, South must hope that East began with the defensive club guard.

South cashes his diamonds as before. On the last round of diamonds, East must discard his remaining heart to avoid giving up an immediate trick. Dummy's top clubs are cashed and East is thrown in with a third round of clubs. East is forced to lead a spade, giving South a third finesse in that suit.
This sort of squeeze, when a defender is forced to give up a link to his partner's hand so that he can be endplayed, matures with exactly 2 losers.

notes: West leads the ♠2 against 7♠. There are only 11 top tricks (6 spades, the ♥A, the ♦A, and 3 clubs). If clubs are 3-3, 13 tricks will be easy. South should concentrate on trying to overcome a 4-2 or worse club break.

If clubs are not breaking, the only chance will be a squeeze. The only possible squeeze is a 3-suit repeating squeeze. One of the defenders will have to hold the ♥K and the ♦K, as well as length in clubs.

South should win the opening lead, draw a second round of trump, cash the ♥A, and ♦A. South next runs his spades. On the play of the last spade a diamond can be pitched from dummy and East is squeezed. A club discard will give up 2 tricks immediately. A discard of the ♥K or ♦K will set up a trick for South. The play of that winner will squeeze East again.

3-suit squeezes generally need specific entry and threat requirements in order to repeat. Dummy's extended threat in clubs and the presence of 2 threats in the opposite hand allow the above position to gain 2 tricks regardless of which defender is threatened in the 3 suits.

If East has length in clubs, South may be able to neutralize West's trump holding with the rare smother play. After finessing again in hearts, a club is played to dummy and a spade is ruffed. Another club is played to dummy and dummy's last spade is ruffed. South cashes 3 diamond tricks and exits with a club. West must discard and East wins the trick.

East must return either a spade or a diamond. South ruffs and West's "certain trump trick" is smothered into oblivion. If West chooses to underruff, dummy discards and the ♥A will win at trick 13. If, instead, West plays the ♥K, dummy can overruff and South's remaining heart will win the last trick.

notes: West leads the ♠6 against 6♥. West's lead is in response to his partner's preempt and South must win the ♠A. A heart finesse wins, but East's discard reveals what looks like a certain trump trick for West. There is also a certain spade loser.
This deal looks superficially similar to the last one, C-26. In that deal, South was able to neutralize West's trump holding in this situation with the help of a smother play.

In an attempt to do the same thing here, suppose that South continues by taking another heart finesse, cashing the ♦A, playing a diamond, and ruffing. Dummy is entered with the ♣A and another diamond is ruffed.

South next cashes the remaining clubs pitching a spade from dummy on the last round (West must have at least 4 clubs for the contract to have a chance). If South exits with a spade, West will discard his last diamond and East will win. East's diamond return will kill the smother play as West will be able to overruff with the ♥K as dummy must follow.

It would have done no good to discard a diamond from dummy on the fourth round of clubs. In fact, pitching a spade was necessary and South can succeed (though not with a smother play) in the above position. West counts out to 1444 distribution. South can lead a heart to the ♥A and play dummy's remaining diamond, ruffing as West follows. South has taken the first twelve tricks. The defensive spade and trump tricks will fall together at trick 13.

notes: West leads the ♦K against 7♥. The diamond lead gives South an opportunity to make a big decision at trick 1. If the ♦A is played, South has 2 possible losers he can discard. South can discard the ♠Q and play for clubs to be 3-3. Alternatively, South can discard a club and play for the spade finesse to be working.

South can avoid making this decision until he knows what to discard. The ♦2 should be played from dummy and ruffed by South. South's basic plan should be to draw trump and cash 3 rounds of clubs ending in dummy.

If clubs prove to be 3-3, South's fourth club will be high and the ♠Q can be discarded on the ♦A. If a defender discards on the third round of clubs, South can discard his fourth club on the ♦A and take the spade finesse. This is an example of a Discovery Play. Discovery Play involves testing one suit so that it will be known what line of play should be taken.

South can improve on this plan be cashing all of the hearts (discarding spades from the dummy) before playing clubs. If, on the third round of clubs, West discards, the ♦A will squeeze East. East must keep his club guard and, therefore, must come down to a singleton spade as South discards his club loser.
When a spade is played from dummy and East follows small, West must have the ♠K as East's last card is known to be a club. South should play the ♠A and hope that West began with a singleton ♠K.

notes: West leads the ♦Q against 7♠. West's lead is won by South with the ♦A. South must find a way to dispose of his diamond loser and, at the same time, avoid losing a trump trick.

It would be a mistake to ruff the ♦2 in dummy at trick 2. If South then continued by cashing the ♠A and West dropped the ♠J or ♠10, South would have to take a second round trump finesse to pick up East's trumps in the above layout. This play would have disastrous consequences if West began with both honours in spades.
Cashing a top spade in hand can also lead to problems. If West plays the ♠J or ♠10, South will have to continue a spade to the ♠A in case East began with 4 spades.

If both defenders follow to the second round of spades, South might fail when spades are 3-2. If South crosses in hearts and plays the ♦2, ruffing, South will have to return to the closed hand to draw the last trump. Trying to ruff a club risks a trump promotion and attempting to cross in hearts risks a defensive ruff.
South should cash the ♠A on the first round of trump. If West follows small, South must hope that trumps are 3-2. South crosses in spades, ruffs the ♦2 and crosses in hearts to draw the last trump.

If West follows with the ♠J or ♠10 on the first round of trump, a second trump is played to the closed hand. If West follow, the play continues as before. If West discards, the club finesse is necessary.
The club finesse should be taken and the ♣A cashed. If East follows, the ♦2 is discarded and South can draw East's trumps with a finesse.
If the ♣A is ruffed by East, South can overruff, ruff the ♦2 in dummy, and cross in hearts to draw East's last trump.

notes: West leads the ♦J against 4♥. West's opening lead should be won by South. South has no reason to delay drawing trump. East wins the third round of trump and returns a diamond. South wins this trick as West discards.

At first glance, the position looks bleak. It seems that South has a certain diamond loser and that clubs will have to be played for just 1 loser. By proper technique, South can succeed in a number of cases where 2 club losers exist. West's inability to lead diamonds could mean trouble for the defense.

South should continue by leading the ♣9 or ♣8 to the ♣A. When East drops an honour, presumably a singleton or from ♣K ♣Q doubleton, prospects have improved. South should lead a spade honour from dummy, planning to discard his diamond loser if East follows low. When East covers, South ruffs.

South should continue the ♣9. If East began with a doubleton ♣K ♣Q, South will have succeeded in playing clubs for 1 loser and will not mind losing a diamond trick. If East began with a singleton honour in clubs, West has no good answer.
If West allows South to win this trick, South will play another club. After cashing his 2 club tricks, West will be forced to play a spade to dummy.
If West wins the ♣10 and cashes a top club, South must be careful to unblock the ♣J. Dummy will now have a club entry for the spade winner.

There are several possible layouts of the defenders' clubs that will allow this line of play to succeed. Here are a few of them: (a), (b), and (c). If West has this last club holding, South can succeed without risking the ruffing spade finesse. If West has the above hand (d), however, making the ruffing spade finesse wrong, he would have overcalled 1♠.

If, when South plays the first round of clubs, West plays the ♣K or ♣Q, South will have to guess how to proceed. It is probably right to win the ♣A and play a club towards the closed hand, planning on playing the ♣J if East follows low. By playing this way, South will lose only when West was dealt ♣K ♣Q doubleton.
